p: Sam Okafor has run the Halcyon for almost two years, and the crew launches January 9.
At the readiness board in December he refused to sign Tallgrass's waiver calling the valve's ground runs nominal, and filed his reasons in writing.
Ruth Calder told the board in public how she signed the Petrel's waiver in 2035, and Garrett put his own 2059 phone call to Hana into the record.

The board deferred the choice to a final test of MOIV-1 on orbit on January 30, with criteria published first, a replacement valve flying up with the crew, and crew risk accepted only by the board with the crew's written consent.
Sam told Ada everything about Leo Marchetti and the jet in Arizona, including that he'll never know.
Esther Quayle. Chair of the Independent Readiness Board, with thirty years on a range safety console.
Yusra Haddad. Halcyon's commander, and now the product owner of the flight software backlog.
Ruth Calder. On the readiness board.
Quinn Abernathy. Sam's deputy and the countdown lead.
Dr. Anjali Rao. The doctor on Halcyon's crew.
Lorna Whitcombe. The ARA's flight operations director.
Tuesday, January 2. 5:40 AM. The high bay at Watkins was empty, which Sam had known it would be, and he walked into it anyway.

All three modules had gone by the first week of December, and the floor where they'd stood for three years was swept and bare, with the yellow tape of their footprints still on the epoxy. The overhead crane was parked at the north wall with its hook drawn all the way up. Somebody had left the pallet jack Garrett gave his speeches from in the middle of the floor, and it looked like a thing that had been forgotten at a party.
Over the doors the clock said 47.

Mars was a little over thirteen minutes away by light this morning, and getting closer every day, the way it had been since summer. The crew had been in quarantine at the Cape since the day after Christmas, all four of them in crew quarters with a window onto a parking lot, and Yusra Haddad, the commander, had sent a photograph on New Year's Eve of her four kids on the other side of the glass, holding up a sign that said 2063 in glitter.
He'd spent New Year's Eve at the kitchen table in Aurora, with page thirteen and a pencil. The envelope to Ruth was still on the counter by the door, under his keys, unsealed.

Across the road in the program room, Quinn had the whiteboard the way she'd left it before Christmas. TEST TUE JAN 30, boxed. Under it, since Sunday, a second line in her small capitals. CRITERIA BEFORE DATA. WED 0900, FEDERAL BUILDING. Under that, in Hana's handwriting: Write the limit before you see the trace.

Ruth's console log. Petrel. After. L Plus 366 Days. June 12 2036. oh four ten, cape. beach road. rental car. parked where the vans parked last year. nobody here. oh four thirty, walked to the water. lifeguard stand. number 7. sat on the step. oh four thirty five, 366. leap year. a year and a day. it took the year a day longer to get here. oh six hundred, the poll. said the stations in order, out loud, to the water. prop first. left a second where the second was. oh six thirty one, liftoff, a year ago. a pelican went over. I let it. oh nine twenty one, ignition. 0938 cutoff. sat through it. oh nine thirty nine, LOS. said it. nobody on the loop. ten hundred, wrote the report in one line. 400 pages. one line. ten oh one, we had the data. we didn't have the nerve. eleven hundred, a woman with a dog asked if I was all right. eleven hundred, said yes. heard how I said it. eleven oh one, said no. eleven oh two, she sat down. the dog too. we didn't talk. thirteen hundred, drove back. 1001 line stands.

Wednesday, January 3. 9:00 AM. The board's small room on the fourth floor, not the hearing room. No camera and no gallery, and a whiteboard somebody had cleaned badly, so last month's arrows still showed through like old tire tracks.

Esther Quayle sat at the end of the table with a kitchen timer in front of her. Ruth was two seats down, in the gray cardigan, with the green pen. Lorna Whitcombe had brought her propulsion officer, a young man with a laptop and very straight posture. Garrett and Hana sat for Tallgrass. Sam and Quinn sat for the program. On the screen at the far end, from crew quarters at the Cape, were all four of the crew, and behind Yusra somebody's drawing of a rocket with four stick figures waving from the windows was taped to the wall.

The decision says criteria set with the program, the crew, and flight operations, and published before the test, the chair said. I'd like them published by noon on Friday the twelfth. Nobody in this room knows what MOIV-1 will do on the thirtieth. That's why we're doing this today.

What they did know was on Quinn's first page. Thirty nine completed closes on the ground valve since November. Every third close after a soak had a ripple starting two milliseconds after lift, and the position channels disagreed for a few milliseconds. All of it was inside the ten millisecond ground acceptance limit. Hot fire 2's cycle three, which he'd kept through a hurricane: seven milliseconds, inside ten. October's forty milliseconds on orbit, on the valve that would fly. Harness revision C against D, unexplained.

Garrett had a proposal on one page, and he presented it well. Use the limits the valve was accepted to. Ten milliseconds, everywhere. If it meets them, the workaround flies. The valve was built to those numbers, and that's the cleanest standard there is. Hana didn't look up from her notes. Ten is a ground acceptance limit for a warm stand. Nobody ever wrote one for a cold valve on orbit. And on orbit it already did forty. Ten fails the valve you're hoping passes.

On the screen Yusra leaned toward the camera. Whatever the numbers are, I'd like to know before we see a trace what each answer does. Inside, then what. Outside, then what. I don't want to be working that out at two in the afternoon on the thirtieth.

Ruth Calder, who'd flown the Petrel and lost it, said one thing, to the table and not to anyone at it. The hardest line to write is the one about what you'll do if you get the answer you don't want. Write that one first. Then she wrote something on her pad and turned it over. Quinn had a draft table from New Year's night in the folder on her knee.

Quinn puts the table on the screen and Sam walks it. Six criteria, numbered C1 to C6 down the side, each with its measurement, its limit, and a line on where the limit comes from. C1 is the one everybody's here for: position disagreement at most fifteen milliseconds, a third of the forty five at which the cutoff sequence calls the valve failed, with the ten millisecond ground limit reported beside it. Then pressure confirming the close, MOIV-2 on every cutoff, the procedure as written, the soak by body temperature, and last, every channel recorded and two blind readers who agree. Then the rules, lettered. Rule A: all six met makes the workaround eligible for the board's acceptance, with the crew's consent, and nothing more. Rule B: any one missed, or not measured, starts the spacewalk the next morning. Rule C: every value gets published as measured. Rule D: nothing changes after Friday. Garrett asks where fifteen came from, if not from the ground runs. The chair answers before Sam can. From the cutoff sequence, Mr. Lyle. Forty five milliseconds and a factor of three. It was fifteen before anybody in this room saw a trace, and it would be fifteen whatever the ground runs had shown. She reads the table twice and edits three words. Yusra asks for the eligible line in capitals. Friday the twelfth, then, the chair says, and sets her timer.
Thursday, January 4. 11:10 AM. The form came from Hale's deputy, with a short note on top and a deadline under it in bold.

ARES RELIEF AUTHORITY CREW RISK CONSENT MOIV-1 (DRAFT FOR SIGNATURE BEFORE CREW LAUNCH). I, THE UNDERSIGNED MEMBER OF THE HALCYON CREW, CONSENT TO FLY MOIV-1 WITH THE CR 62-311 WORKAROUND IF THE INDEPENDENT READINESS BOARD ACCEPTS THE RESIDUAL RISK.. SIGNATURE: ________ DATE: ________. RETURN BY 1700 FRIDAY, JANUARY 5.

The note said a consent from orbit would cost a day on January 31, because it needed an uplink, a downlink, and a witness. If the crew signed in quarantine now, the board could accept the risk the afternoon of the test and nobody would lose anything.
Quinn read it over his shoulder. The board's rule says written consent of the crew. It doesn't say when. Hale's office is reading that as anytime.

At 11:40 Yusra called from the Cape. She'd got her copy at the same time he had, and she had the board's draft criteria open beside it, with the word ELIGIBLE in capitals where she'd asked for it. They sent us a form, Sam. Before the data. I'd like to know who's asking us, and what we'd be agreeing to, because I can't tell from this. Behind her, Dr. Anjali Rao, the crew's doctor, said something he didn't catch. Yusra turned, and Anjali leaned into the frame. I said four people in quarantine five days before launch aren't the best judges of what they'd sign later. I'm one of them.

Hale's deputy argues for a day and then stops. Lorna's team builds a ninety minute consent pass into the timeline for the first evening after the board sits: the measured values uplinked by 5 PM on test day, the board's members on the loop, and each crew member asked separately, on a private channel, by the chair, with Anjali asked first about the crew's condition. A no is recorded as a no and nothing else, and the minutes say so in advance. Yusra reads the plan from the Cape. Ask us each. Not me for them.
Friday, January 5. 7:30 AM. Flight control at Watkins, the planning room behind Lorna's floor.

Quinn had the on orbit timeline on the wall, from docking on Wednesday, January 10, to the burn on Sunday, February 18. Checkout of the habitat and the Breather module until the 29th. The cold soak from 4 PM on Monday, January 29. The test at 2 PM on the 30th. Then two paths. The workaround, which needed no crew time. The spacewalk, which needed nine days of it: two spacewalks and a retest, January 31 to February 8, if everything for it was ready the morning after the test.

It wasn't ready yet. Getting ready was three and a half days of crew time: suits fit checked, the airlock run through, the replacement valve out of its case and inspected, tools staged, one rehearsal in the trainer. If that waited until after the result, the spacewalk path was thirteen days, not nine.
Hale's office had sent its own idea overnight: cut the soak to eight hours and run the test on Friday the 26th, which would give back four days to whichever path the board chose.

Yusra had sent a request of her own from the Cape, and it was harder to wave off. If the test can run on the 26th, the crew gets three days of rest before burn prep instead of none. We'd like that, if it's safe.

Garrett had his own note, one line. Don't spend 3.5 crew days preparing for a spacewalk we won't need. Lorna, whose team would fly the ship, read it and capped her marker. Whatever we pick goes on my wall by noon, and once it's on my wall it's mine.
The window ran to March 4. The fourteen days after the 18th were in the plan as a declared reserve, boxed in Quinn's handwriting since July of 2061, and so far nobody had touched them.

Lorna moves the three and a half days into the checkout weeks, in blocks that don't touch the soak or the test: suits on the 15th, the airlock on the 18th, the valve out of its case on the 22nd, the rehearsal on the 25th. If the test misses, the first spacewalk starts Wednesday morning and the path ends February 8. If it passes, the crew has spent three and a half days on a spacewalk nobody makes. Quinn writes INSURANCE beside the blocks in her own capitals. Garrett reads it and doesn't send another note.
Monday, January 8. 9:20 AM. The crew would launch in the morning, and the cards would launch with them.

There were two procedures: the workaround's conditioning cycle and cutoff, revision F, and the January 30 test, which used most of the same steps. They'd be on the crew's tablets and printed on cards in a binder clipped to the bulkhead, because Yusra wanted paper for anything she'd do with her hand on a switch.

At seven Quinn had run the last inspection with flight operations' procedure editor, line by line against the ground runs. She'd found three things. Step 14 commanded MOIV-2 closed before the conditioning cycle finished; on the ground runs it had been after. The crew display labeled MOIV-1's two position channels A and B and didn't say which ran through the revision C harness. And the ripple limit on card 6 still said twelve milliseconds, from a draft in November.
The procedure had been written from Wendell's runs, and some of his notes were still in the margins, in capitals.

Tallgrass's procedures office wanted to fix the three tonight and sign the revision. They're right that it's three lines, Hana said. I'd like to know why we found three today and not in December. Quinn didn't say anything. She'd been asking herself the same thing since seven.

They do it at eleven that morning, on video with crew quarters at the Cape, every step out loud. At step 22 Ilse Brandvold, the pilot, stops them. The callout says MOIV-2 OPEN when the switch it points to reads CLOSE in the cockpit graphic. A fourth. Revision G goes under configuration control at 1:40 PM. On the 17th Lorna's people run it in the ground sim, and on the 18th the crew runs it in the trainer aboard Halcyon, and both runs match the ground valve's sequence step for step. Hana asks the procedures office for a note on why the December review missed three, and gets one.

Tuesday, January 9. 4:12 AM in Watkins, 6:12 at the Cape. He watched the crew launch on the big screen in flight control with Lorna's controllers, who didn't clap until the vehicle was in orbit, and then clapped once, together, like a single door closing. Yusra's four kids had been at the viewing site with their father and a sign. The replacement valve rode in its case in the cargo bay. On Wednesday at 7:40 PM the crew docked with Halcyon and opened the hatch, and Yusra's first call down was a pressure reading.
Thursday, January 11. 5:40 AM. The kitchen in Aurora, with the coffee maker going. One way twelve minutes and forty three seconds.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 4229. One way, 12 minutes 43 seconds. Margin, 229 days. Hi, Dad. Log fifty nine. We watched the launch. All of us, in the galley, thirteen minutes behind you. When it cleared the tower Okonkwo cried, which she'll deny, so don't tell her I told you. Yusra's bunk in C ring is made up. Malik put a sign on it that says RESERVED in letters you can read from the hatch. Okay. Here's the log I've been not recording for twenty one months. Bay D is done. I finished it in July, three weeks past your three point number, which on Mars is early. Racks full, air handler balanced. Mom's peppers are four feet tall in the warm corner, and they're ugly, and they're the best thing up here. It hasn't been in my number for a reason. It runs sealed, on its own handler, because putting a bay on the main loop takes the director's signature, and a bay nobody approved doesn't get one. Sealed, it's starved. Plants need what we breathe out, and the main loop is where all the breathing is. So it's been making a little, and Pilar and I have been putting the little into the two old lander tanks behind it, with a compressor that would give the safety officer a heart attack. The tanks are full. Seventeen days of reserve in them, by the gauges, which we've read every sol since October. On the main loop it does better. I ran it on the loop six nights in December, on Pilar's shifts, and fit a line. If the loop does what six nights say, it makes about twenty four more days of air before the nutrient salts run out. That's a quarter of a day for every day it runs, and the salts last ninety six days. Forty one, with the tanks. I didn't count it before, because a number they can shut you out of isn't a number, and because six nights is a fit, not a measurement. You taught me that, with the spreadsheets, though you didn't mean to. I'm putting it in now because the ship's coming and the end of the window matters, and because somebody on Earth needs to check my line before anybody leans on it. I told Hollis at seven this morning, in his office, with the gauge log. He didn't say anything for a long time. Then he asked me to show him. The safety officer inspects on Saturday. If it passes, we're on the loop Sunday. Mine's 270 with it. And the ship gets here on day 238. Dad, that's plus thirty two. I've never written plus. Not once since I started counting. And if the ship goes on the last day of the window, it's still plus with Bay D. Without it, it isn't. That's the one I've been carrying around. Don't count it until somebody checks it. I mean that. Love you. Log fifty nine. Ada out.
He watched it three times. The third time he stopped it on the gauge log in her hands, a spiral notebook with a cover that had been blue once, every page full.

He'd known since April of 2061. She'd told him about the bay in a log, and he'd asked her for three numbers, and she'd given him nine, fourteen, and twenty two months, and he'd written them on a sticky note inside the cabinet door over the coffee maker, where it still was, curling. He'd known in August of that year, when she'd asked him not to hand her over. He'd kept it, because she'd asked him to. He'd never once put it in front of anybody who was making a decision.

For two years he'd been running a ship to rescue her. She'd been building her own way out, a rack at a time, on hours she didn't have, and writing minus nine at the bottom of every log because she wouldn't count what she couldn't prove.
The program's status went to Hale and the board's clerk at noon every Thursday. Its margin line said 236, minus two.

He writes it at the kitchen table and sends it at 9:12. DISCLOSURE, S. OKAFOR, PROGRAM MANAGER. Five sentences. An unrostered hydroponics bay on Ares Station, built by its own staff, which he's known about since April 2061 from his daughter's personal logs. Its output was never in her stated margin or the program's. He didn't report it. The station's director was told today by the people who built it. He asks the ARA's mission assurance office to check the bay's data before the program counts a day of it. Hale calls at 9:30 and is angry for four minutes, then asks how sure anybody is. He says that's not his to be sure of. At the program room Quinn reads the memo, says nothing, and draws a second line on the margin chart in pencil, dotted, and writes UNVERIFIED beside it. That night he records a log at the kitchen table and doesn't play it back first. I told Hale this morning that I've known about Bay D since April of '61. I'm telling you the same day. You wrote plus. I've watched it four times now. I've been building a ship to come get you, and you've been building the door.
Monday, January 15. 6:30 AM. Hollis Bayne's Monday report posted to the ARA's site, the way it had every Monday for three years. It was longer than usual.

ARES STATION DIRECTOR'S WEEKLY REPORT TO THE ARA MONDAY, JANUARY 15, 2063 (EXTRACT). OXYGEN PLANT OPERATING WITHIN PROJECTED DEGRADATION.. MARGIN: 232 DAYS (ARA MODEL).. BAY D (HYDROPONICS, C RING): AN UNAUTHORIZED MODIFICATION, BUILT BY A. OKAFOR AND HER TEAM. REPORTED TO THIS OFFICE BY ITS BUILDER, SOL 4229. INSPECTED BY STATION SAFETY, SOL 4231. ACCEPTED WITH THREE CORRECTIONS: COMPRESSOR RELOCATED, TANK RELIEF VALVES REPLACED, FIRE DETECTION ADDED. TIED INTO THE MAIN AIR LOOP, SOL 4232.. CREDIT: 41 DAYS (17 STORED, BY GAUGE; 24 PROJECTED). NOT INCLUDED IN THE MARGIN ABOVE. PENDING ARA MISSION ASSURANCE REVIEW.. A. OKAFOR IS NAMED BAY D LEAD. A NOTE OF THE UNAUTHORIZED WORK IS IN HER FILE. A NOTE IS IN MINE.. SHE HID IT BECAUSE I WOULD HAVE SHUT IT. THE RULE THAT MADE THAT TRUE WAS MINE, AND IT IS WITHDRAWN. ANY RESIDENT MAY NOW PROPOSE A MODIFICATION TO THIS OFFICE AND WILL HAVE AN ANSWER IN SEVEN SOLS.. MORALE: I HAVE WRITTEN STRONG IN THIS LINE FOR THREE YEARS. THIS WEEK IT IS BETTER THAN THAT.

Sam read it twice at the counter. Beside it was page fourteen, which had come on Saturday in a long white envelope with a Golden postmark, posted the afternoon the board's criteria went up on Friday and not an hour before. He'd read the 1001 line standing exactly where he was standing now. We had the data. We didn't have the nerve.

Ruth had called on Sunday night, which she'd never done about the board's business. She kept it to the criteria. I voted for them. I've read them four times since, and I'm going to stop. Read them once more before the thirtieth, Sam, and then don't read them again until the numbers are in. Don't let anybody read them to you on the day. He said he wouldn't. That's all. Good night. She hung up before he could ask her anything, and he hadn't been going to.

At the program room Quinn had the station's engineering packet up. The station's Breather team had sent it on January 8, before the crew left Earth, and item two named the station's benefits owner: Chiamaka Okonkwo, Breather operations, reporting through the director's packet. Item three was a question. Bay D changes the arithmetic. If its air is counted in the Breather's number, Earth will think the plant is better than it is. If the plant's air is counted in Bay D's, Ada gets a statue. Which line is which?
Whatever had been said in December about what success was, nobody had written down how to count air from two places.

There were other ideas. Hale's program office wanted the benefit reported as Halcyon delivered and the Breather installed by September 6, with a box to tick. Hollis's office had sent a single figure: station margin above 180 days on the ninetieth sol after arrival. The ARA's model, rebuilt in July, could compute a benefit from Earth without anybody on the station lifting a pen. Halcyon's cargo module carried seed stock and nutrient salts, so Bay D would start again when the ship arrived, and its air would go into the same tanks as the Breather's.
Under the packet, Quinn had pinned his disclosure memo from Thursday. Somebody at the ARA had written VERIFYING in the margin.

It takes two packets, because the station answers a day later. What comes back is a half page and a table. The baseline is the reserve on the day the Breather starts. The measure is the reserve itself, read from the station's plant log every sol, not the model. Bay D gets its own line, and so does the Breather, so that neither borrows the other's air. The target is the reserve rising instead of falling for ninety sols. Two sols of falling reserve in a row triggers a review with Lorna's team. Chiamaka owns it and reports every week through the director's packet to the board. Assumptions and risks are listed underneath, salts and spares and gauge drift among them. Hollis signs the packet. Chiamaka's reply has a line at the bottom. Understood as: we measure air, not ships.

Wednesday, January 17. 8:00 AM. Flight control. The crew had been aboard Halcyon for a week, and Lorna had a number on her whiteboard in red: 84. Crew hours left before the soak, outside the checkout and the spacewalk preparation.
Under it, Quinn had stuck up nine cards, one for each request that had come in since launch. Each said who wanted it and how many crew hours it took.

CREW TIME REQUESTS JAN 17 TO JAN 29 84 HOURS AVAILABLE. 1. FULL REGRESSION, FLIGHT LOAD 11.6, ON THE FLIGHT COMPUTERS (RAFA, THANDI): 6. 2. BREATHER MODULE THERMAL CHECKOUT (PALOMA'S TEAM): 12. 3. LANDER HEALTH CHECK (LANDER TEAM): 8. 4. CABIN CAMERA INSTALL FOR THE BURN BROADCAST (ARA PUBLIC AFFAIRS): 10. 5. SECOND SPACEWALK REHEARSAL (EVA TEAM): 16. 6. MEDICAL BASELINES (DR. RAO): 6. 7. BACKUP COMMUNICATIONS PATH TEST (FLIGHT OPS): 8. 8. HABITAT STOWAGE AUDIT (CARGO TEAM): 20. 9. CARGO PHOTO SURVEY FOR THE FAMILIES' NEWSLETTER (FAMILIES OF ARES): 5. TOTAL: 91 HOURS. OVER BY 7. PLUS 40 FOR ITEMS 2 AND 8 IF THEY'RE DONE THE WAY THEIR TEAMS WANT.
Really it was a hundred and thirty one, because the Breather team and the cargo team had each sent a short version and a long one.
Item one had been on every list since the workaround was approved. Thandi wanted all six hours, on the flight computers, not the bench.

On the screen from orbit, Yusra had her sleeves pushed up and a pen clipped to her collar. We'll do whatever's on the list. I'd like the list to be the right list. Beside her, Mateo Echeverría, the flight engineer, held up a hand with a bandage on one thumb, from a stowage latch. And not fourteen hour days. We tried one Tuesday. By the end of it I'd stowed a wrench in the trash bag.

They go card by card, with Yusra on the screen and Lorna at the board, and ask one question of each: if this found a problem, would anybody decide anything differently before the burn? Regression: yes, it's the burn's software, all six hours on the flight computers. The second spacewalk rehearsal: yes. The Breather's thermal checkout, short version: yes. Backup communications: yes. Medical baselines: yes, Anjali says, flatly. The lander check moves to cruise week two. Half the stowage audit and the photo survey go to cruise too. The cabin camera comes out, and Sam calls Hale's office himself before lunch to say why. Fifty eight hours of eighty four. Yusra initials the board from orbit, which is to say she holds up her initials on a card and Quinn copies them.

Friday, January 19. 9:00 AM. The ARA's integrated readiness review, the last one before the poll, in the big room at flight control. Hale in the chair for the agency. Lorna, Garrett, Hana, Corinne, Rafa, the crew on the loop, two of the partners' liaisons, and an observer from the board's staff at the back with a notebook.

The first item wasn't on the agenda. The ARA's mission assurance office had checked Bay D's gauge log and the six night runs, and it adopted the forty one days at 9:05, with a footnote: seventeen days verified by gauge, twenty four projected and to be remeasured every week. The agency's line went to plus thirty nine, the first plus on it since July. Hale read the footnote out loud and then the name in it, and didn't look at Sam.

Then Quinn's tracker, twenty three open items. Most were small. One belonged to the ARA's sustainability office. After the burn, the spent departure stage had to be pushed onto a heliocentric disposal path, with propellant set aside for it. The plan for that was written and costed, and not yet signed. Four said CLOSED PENDING PAPERWORK. One was I-62-117, MOIV-1, with the test date beside it.

Hana had a slide on it she wasn't sure she should show. The second test article's life test in Building 6 had passed 2,900 cycles. At 2,400 her borescope had found a polished ring on the seat that hadn't been there at 1,800. The root cause team had a hypothesis. Hana wasn't ready to call it a finding, and she said so twice.

Garrett had a proposal for the chart, and he put it kindly. The program's ready. The valve is the board's call, not ours. Put I-62-117 on the board's list where it belongs, close the four that are only waiting on signatures, and let the partners see what we've actually built. One green box, Sam. They've earned one. One of the liaisons nodded.

Quinn puts all twenty three on one screen, each with its criterion, its evidence, its owner, and its date. The four closed pending paperwork go back to open, and three of them close by Tuesday with the paperwork in hand. I-62-117 sits in the middle, open, with the test on the 30th and what each answer does beside it: a pass goes to the board, a miss starts the spacewalk on Wednesday. Each path has its dates. Lorna says two of her own conditions are still open and reads them out. Hale reads the screen top to bottom, the way she'd count a roll call, and asks the liaisons to take a picture of this one. Garrett gets no green box. At the break he tells Corinne it's a better chart than the one he wanted, which Corinne writes on her legal pad.

Tuesday, January 23. 1:00 PM. The full countdown rehearsal for the burn, in flight control, with Lorna's twelve controllers, the program's consoles, and the crew on the loop from orbit. Quinn ran it from the countdown lead's desk with the procedure open in front of her and a cup of tea she forgot about at 1:05. Ilse flew the simulated burn.

At T minus twenty minutes Quinn called the poll. Each station answered in turn. When she got to propulsion, Arlo, at Wendell's old console, said, Prop is and stopped, and then said, go, and Quinn moved on to guidance, because the next name on her sheet was guidance.

At simulated cutoff, MOIV-2 closed on command. Lorna had put in a failure nobody knew about: channel B on MOIV-1 dropped out at cutoff. Two consoles missed it for forty seconds, because three people were talking on the loop at once. It turned out Quinn's poll sheet listed the stations in a different order from the procedure, which nobody had noticed in four practice runs.

Afterward, in the hall by the vending machine, Arlo found Sam. I had a question about MOIV-2's data rate. That was the pause. I didn't want to hold up the poll. It was a sim. He tucked his hands into his jacket. I'd have asked it on the real one. Probably.
Sam stood there with a bag of pretzels he didn't want and thought about page ten, and the second somebody had heard in 2035 and never asked about.

The rehearsal's list had fourteen items on it by four o'clock. Friday's second rehearsal was on the timeline, and Hale's office had asked by email whether it could go, since it took three hours of the crew's attention four days before the test.

They do it at seven in the controllers' break room, with pizza, and Lorna says the ground rule before anyone sits down: nobody here is in trouble. What did you see, and what did you need? Arlo tells the room about the pause himself. Lorna says she's done the same thing twice, on lander polls, and never told anybody. Three changes come out of it. Any console may answer hold, question, and it doesn't count against the go/no-go. The countdown lead asks any pause to say again its status. One voice on the loop during the poll; side questions go to a second loop. Quinn writes them into the countdown procedure that night and sends them to the ARA's procedures office as a change to its standard countdown, for every ship after this one. On Friday two consoles pause, and Quinn asks each of them to say again. Both times it's nothing. Ilse Brandvold, the pilot, says on the loop, Flight, crew. Same rule up here. If one of us pauses, ask.
Thursday, January 25. 6:00 AM. Quinn had been in since five, and the chart on her screen had two lines on it that had come apart.

The crew's checkout plan was four hundred task points from January 10 to January 29, twenty days. At the end of Wednesday, day fifteen, they'd earned 236. The plan said 284. On the plan, 236 had been due halfway through day thirteen.

Crew checkout: planned points by end of day, and earned at day 15. Plan: 400 points from Wed Jan 10 (day 1) to Mon Jan 29 (day 20). Earned at the end of day 15, Wed Jan 24: 236. Of the 164 points left, 41 must be done before the soak starts at 4 PM on the 29th; they're on plan.

It had started on Saturday with a coolant pump on the habitat's loop B, which had begun to make a noise like gravel in a coffee can. Mateo had spent nineteen hours on it over three days and fixed it, and two of his fingers were still taped. The medical baselines had taken twice as long as planned, because Anjali didn't skip things.
The work that had to be done before the soak was on plan; Quinn had kept it that way on purpose. The rest of the checkout wasn't.

Garrett's note proposed fourteen hour days through Monday. Hale's office asked whether the test could move to Saturday, February 3. Corinne had sent a text at 5:52. My second shift can take every bit of telemetry reduction and procedure prep the crew's doing by hand. Twenty two points. Say the word. Lorna had a list of her own on the whiteboard, headed NOT NEEDED BEFORE THE BURN. Some of it had been on the list since the day they sorted the eighty four hours.

Lorna and Yusra go through the 123 points that aren't test critical, line by line, on the loop. Fifty eight aren't needed before the burn, and they move to cruise weeks one to three, owned by flight ops in writing. Corinne's second shift at Watkins takes twenty two more off the crew: telemetry reduction and the procedure prep they'd been doing by hand. The crew stays on ten hour days, and Anjali's rest rule holds. Quinn redraws the chart with two plans on it, one for before the burn and one for cruise, and the line for before the burn meets its plan on February 1. The forty one test critical points finish Sunday, a day early.
Friday, January 26. 10:00 AM. Hale's office had a plan for Monday night, and it came with a run of show.

A press event in Denver at seven, with families in the front rows. The first item: ARA SUPPORTED STATION INITIATIVE EXTENDS COLONY MARGIN BY 41 DAYS. The second: a live broadcast of Tuesday's test from Halcyon's cabin, with a countdown graphic and the commander narrating each close. The cabin camera was already out of the crew's timeline, so the plan said the camera would go back in.
Simon Greaves had sent one line at 9:15. What happens Tuesday if it's fourteen milliseconds?

Frances Odum called at 9:40. The families in her group had two hundred questions, she said, and most of them were one question: what does Tuesday mean? And there was a second thing. The station families have been sending messages home all week about a bay full of peppers. They call it Ada's bay. Is it real, and why isn't her name on anything the agency's put out?
It was in Hollis's report. It wasn't in Hale's run of show.

It takes two calls with Hale and one with Lorna. What goes out is one page, at the same hour, to the families' list and the press: the six criteria, the four rules, both paths and their dates, and when people will hear. Measured values by 6 PM Tuesday, the board's ruling when it sits, and Sam on the families' line the same day it posts. The forty one days are credited to Ada Okafor and the Bay D team on Ares Station, with the station director's safety staff, measured there and checked by the ARA's mission assurance office. There's no cabin camera. The crew works, and the public feed carries flight control's own loop. Greaves runs the page in full on Countdown to Ares and answers his own question on air. Fourteen would pass the fifteen millisecond line, and it wouldn't explain the valve, and they told us so first. Frances texts at 8:40 PM. They're calling it Ada's bay. I told them that's what it's called.
Monday, January 29. 4:00 PM. On orbit, MOIV-1's heaters went off, and the cold soak began. Twenty two hours. Over the high bay doors the clock said 20.

In flight control the room had split without anybody deciding it would. Rafa's team had a sprint goal on their whiteboard in green marker: SPRINT GOAL: TEST PASSES 1/30. Somebody in Tallgrass's propulsion group had ordered T shirts that said PASS IT, and a box of them was open on a chair. Garrett hadn't ordered them, and had said so, and was wearing one.

At the far end of the room the spacewalk support team sat together with their checklists and didn't wear the shirts. One of them had been called the plan B people in a meeting, and it had stuck. They'd spent three and a half crew days getting ready for a morning that might not come.
On the loop from orbit, Ilse asked it plainly. Flight, crew. Question for the program. Are we hoping tomorrow, or testing?
Hana was at her desk with the lot data and her coat on, not leaving.

At seven he gets everyone who'll fit into the room, with the crew on the loop, and takes five minutes. The test is to find out what the valve does. A pass makes the workaround eligible and the board decides. A miss starts the spacewalk at six on Wednesday, and the ship still leaves inside the window. Nobody in this room is on the losing side of tomorrow, and the spacewalk team are the reason a miss isn't a disaster. The goal hasn't changed since January of 2061. It's air at Ares Station. Rafa wipes his whiteboard with his sleeve and writes, SPRINT GOAL: CLEAN DATA 1/30. The T shirts go back in their box, and somebody tapes the box shut. Yusra comes on the loop. Copy. We're testing. Ilse says, Then I'll read the card twice and go to sleep.

Tuesday, January 30. 12:40 PM. Flight control at Watkins, with the wind sock straight out toward Kansas and every chair in the room taken. On the big screen, beside the countdown clock at 19, the criteria that had posted on the twelfth, with the signatures under them. E. QUAYLE FOR THE BOARD S. OKAFOR FOR THE PROGRAM Y. HADDAD FOR THE CREW L. WHITCOMBE FOR FLIGHT OPERATIONS Quinn had drafted the table on New Year's night. The three words the chair had edited were still in the chair's handwriting.

The soak was twenty hours and forty minutes old. MOIV-1's body temperature read where Hana had said it would, and she'd stopped looking at it every thirty seconds and started looking at it every minute.
Rafa's whiteboard said CLEAN DATA 1/30. The box of shirts was under a desk with tape on it.

At 1:30 Wendell came in. Nobody had asked him. He had his canvas jacket on and page twelve in his shirt pocket, behind the doctor's note, and he sat in the back row by the coffee and said to the controller next to him that he'd come to hear it. Arlo saw him from the propulsion console and touched the headset at his ear, and Wendell lifted two fingers off his knee. Nobody asked him anything, and he didn't offer.
Downtown, the board watched from the fourth floor, on the same feed.

At 1:50 Quinn polled the room for the start of the test. At propulsion Arlo said, Prop is go, without a pause. At guidance there was one, a short one, and Quinn said, Guidance, say again your status. It was a headset cable. Everyone in the room heard her ask.
At 1:58 the conditioning cycle ran, exactly as the card said. At 2:00 Yusra's voice came down from orbit, flat and clear. Flight, Halcyon. Close one, on my mark. Mark.

Close one, clean. Close two, clean. The two blind readers at flight operations' propulsion desk sat with their backs to the big screen and their own traces in front of them and wrote on their pads, each turned so the other couldn't see.

Close three. The pressure trace rippled, two milliseconds after lift, the way it had on the ground, the way everybody in the room could have drawn it from memory. The two position channels disagreed for a little while and then agreed again. Downstream pressure said closed at thirty four milliseconds. On orbit MOIV-2 closed on command. Nobody in the room said anything at all. At her desk Hana had the borescope picture from Building 6 open on her second screen, the polished ring at 2,400 cycles, and she didn't look away from it.
Close four, clean. Close five, clean. At 2:31 the readers turned their pads over, and they'd both written the same thing beside close three.

INDEPENDENT READINESS BOARD ITEM 1 FINAL INTEGRATED TEST OF MOIV-1 RESULTS AS MEASURED TUESDAY, JANUARY 30, 2063, 1431. SOAK: 22 HOURS 0 MINUTES BY BODY TEMPERATURE. CLOSES: 5 COMMANDED, 5 COMPLETED.. C1 POSITION DISAGREEMENT, LIMIT 15 MS: CLOSES 1, 2, 4, 5 UNDER 1 MS. CLOSE 3: 12 MS. MET. GROUND ACCEPTANCE LIMIT 10 MS: CLOSE 3 ABOVE IT, REPORTED.. C2 PRESSURE CONFIRMS CLOSED, LIMIT 50 MS: WORST 34 MS, CLOSE 3. MET.. C3 MOIV-2 ON COMMAND AT EVERY CUTOFF: 5 OF 5. MET.. C4 PROCEDURE AS WRITTEN: MET.. C5 SOAK AT LEAST 20 HOURS: MET.. C6 ALL CHANNELS RECORDED, TWO BLIND READERS AGREE: MET. BOTH READERS CALL CLOSE 3.. RIPPLE FROM 2 MS AFTER LIFT, CLOSE 3 ONLY.. RULE A APPLIES. THE WORKAROUND IS ELIGIBLE FOR THE BOARD'S WRITTEN RISK ACCEPTANCE, WITH THE CREW'S WRITTEN CONSENT. ELIGIBLE ISN'T ACCEPTED.. RULE C. CLOSE 3 IS PUBLISHED AS MEASURED. IT PASSES THE 15 MS LIMIT. IT DOESN'T EXPLAIN THE VALVE.. THE BOARD WILL SIT ON THE RESULT.
Lorna told the spacewalk team to keep the suits charged and the valve out of its case until the board said otherwise. They'd done the preparation for a morning that hadn't come yet, and might still.
The consent pass was on the timeline, ninety minutes long, unopened, waiting for whenever the board sat: each of the four, separately, on a private channel, with the data in front of them.

At 5:50 the results page went to the families' list and the press in the same minute, the way he'd said it would. He called Frances at six. She'd already read it twice. Twelve, and the limit's fifteen, and it doesn't explain anything. I can say that. That's what you told us it would look like.
Eleven minutes after the readers turned their pads over, it was on every screen in the galley on Ares Station.
He'd spent the month writing things down before he knew how they'd come out. Today nobody in the room had needed to argue about what a number meant.
That evening Quinn walked back across the road to the program room, to the whiteboard where the box said TEST TUE JAN 30, and under it, in her small capitals, she wrote one number.
Twelve milliseconds on the third close. Inside the limit the board wrote. Above the one the valve was accepted to on the ground. And not zero.
